text: Whoa, look at all these stars. So why is it still this dark out here?
The stars you can actually see with your own eyes? Not that many. In the city, it drops even lower. But our galaxy alone has way, way more than that.
The first person to notice this puzzle wasn't some modern scientist. It was an astronomer, centuries ago.
Except this puzzle isn't named after Kepler at all. It's named after a different astronomer who brought it up again, much later.

Stand in the middle of a thick forest, and look any direction - you'll hit a tree trunk eventually. If the universe went on forever with stars evenly scattered everywhere, every direction you looked would eventually hit a star's surface too.
But the universe is still young, so light from the farthest stars hasn't even reached Earth yet.
Even the sunlight hitting you right now left a few minutes ago. Light from other stars takes a whole lot longer to get here.

And as the universe keeps expanding, light traveling from really far away stretches out along the way, until it fades into colors we can't even see. So there's a theory that some of the galaxies we can see today might eventually fade out of view for good.
The person who first got close to the real answer wasn't a scientist. He wrote horror stories.

So the starlight you're looking at right now already left its star a long, long time ago. Some of it, like the light from the Andromeda galaxy, left before humans even existed. There's also a rumor that some of the stars you're looking at are already gone. But that's almost never actually true - most visible stars still have millions, even billions of years left.
